{'url': 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Sosa', 'title': 'Mercedes Sosa', 'content': 'Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón (9 July 1935 – 4 October 2009) was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout Latin America and many countries outside the region. With her roots in Argentine folk music, Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of El nuevo cancionero. She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice of the voiceless ones",  and often called "the conscience of Latin America".
Sosa performed in venues such as the Lincoln Center in New York City, the Théâtre Mogador in Paris, the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's Carnegie Hall and the Roman Colosseum during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six Latin Grammy awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2004 and two posthumous Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album in 2009 and 2011. She won the Premio Gardel in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for UNICEF.


== Life ==
Sosa was born on 9 July 1935, in San Miguel de Tucumán, in the northwestern Argentine province of Tucumán, of mestizo ancestry. She was of French, Spanish and Diaguita descent. Her nickname "la negra", which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is a reference to her indigenous heritage. Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman, were Peronists, although they never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the Peronist Party in Tucuman under the name Gladys Osorio. In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two months. She recorded her first album, La Voz de la Zafra, in 1959. A performance at the 1965 Cosquín National Folklore Festival—where she was introduced and brought to the stage while sitting in the audience by fellow folk singer Jorge Cafrune— brought her to the attention of the Argentine public. Sosa and her first husband, Manuel Oscar Matus, with whom she had one son, were key players in the mid-60s nueva canción movement (which was called nuevo cancionero in Argentina). Her second record was Canciones con Fundamento, a collection of Argentine folk songs.

Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries. In 1967, Sosa toured the United States and Europe with great success. In later years, she performed and recorded extensively, broadening her repertoire to include material from throughout Latin America.
In the early 1970s, Sosa released two concept albums in collaboration with composer Ariel Ramírez and lyricist Félix Luna: Cantata Sudamericana and Mujeres Argentinas (Argentine Women). She also recorded a tribute to Chilean musician Violeta Parra in 1971, including what was to become one of Sosa's signature songs, Gracias a la vida. She further popularized of songs written by Milton Nascimento of Brazil and Pablo Milanés and Silvio Rodríguez both from Cuba. Throughout the decade, she released albums such as Hasta la Victoria in 1972 and Traigo un Pueblo en mi Voz in 1973. They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by Ariel Petrocelli and Daniel Toro, which tackles political and social issues like wealth and land inequality. During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director Leopoldo Torre Nilsson: El Santo de la Espada in 1970 and Güemes, la tierra en armas in 1971, in which she portrayed Juana Azurduy de Padilla, the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence.

After the military junta of Jorge Videla came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in La Plata in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert. Their release came about through international intervention. Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime. Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to Madrid. She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life. While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter, Patricio Manns. The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland. She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982, several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the Falklands War, and gave a series of concerts at the Teatro Ópera in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A double album of recordings, Mercedes Sosa en Argentina, from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country. In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the Lincoln Center in New York City and the Théâtre Mogador in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998. In 1994, she played in the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City. In 2002, she sold out both Carnegie Hall in New York and the Colosseum in Rome in the same year.

A supporter of Perón, she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President Raul Alfonsin in the election of 1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring" She opposed President Carlos Menem, who was in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of Néstor Kirchner, who became president in 2003.
Sosa was a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Latin America and the Caribbean.
Sosa disliked being identified as a protest singer. While she was outright in her political stances, Sosa said the following on the position of the artist:

“An artist isn’t political in the party political sense – they have a constituency, which is their public – it is the poetry that matters most of all.”
In a career spanning four decades, she worked with performers across several genres and generations, folk, opera, pop, rock, including Martha Argerich, Andrea Bocelli, David Broza, Franco Battiato, Jaime Roos, Joan Baez, Francis Cabrel, Gal Costa, Luz Casal, Lila Downs, Lucio Dalla, Maria Farantouri, Lucecita Benitez, Nilda Fernández, Charly Garcia, León Gieco, Gian Marco, Nana Mouskouri, Pablo Milanés, Holly Near, Milton Nascimento, Pata Negra, Fito Páez, Franco De Vita, Lourdes Pérez, Luciano Pavarotti, Silvio Rodríguez, Ismael Serrano, Shakira, Sting, Caetano Veloso, Julieta Venegas, Gustavo Cerati and Konstantin Wecker
Sosa participated in a 1999 production of Ariel Ramírez's Misa Criolla. Her song Balderrama is featured in the 2008 movie Che, starring Benicio del Toro as the Argentine Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara.
Sosa was the co-chair of the Earth Charter International Commission.


== Awards ==
Sosa won the Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album in 2000 (Misa Criolla), 2003 (Acústico), 2006 (Corazón Libre), 2009 (Cantora 1, which also won Best Recording Package and was nominated for Album of the Year), and 2011 (Deja La Vida Volar), as well as several international awards.
In 1995, Konex Foundation from Argentina granted her the Diamond Konex Award, one of the most prestigious awards in Argentina, as the most important personality in the popular music of her country in the last decade.


== Death ==

Suffering from recurrent endocrine and respiratory problems in later years, the 74-year-old Sosa was hospitalized in Buenos Aires on 18 September 2009. She died from multiple organ failure on 4 October 2009, at 5:15 am. She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March 2019), born of her first marriage. He said: "She lived her 74 years to the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her". The hospital expressed its sympathies to her relatives. Her website featured the following: "Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions leave a great legacy to future generations".
Her body was placed on display at the National Congress building in Buenos Aires for the public to pay their respects, and President Fernández de Kirchner ordered three days of national mourning. Thousands had queued by the end of the day.
Sosa's obituary in The Daily Telegraph said she was "an unrivalled interpreter of works by her compatriot, the Argentine Atahualpa Yupanqui, and Chile's Violeta Parra". Helen Popper of Reuters reported her death by saying she "fought South America's dictators with her voice and became a giant of contemporary Latin American music". Sosa received three Latin Grammy nominations for her album, in 2009 . She went on to win Best Folk Album about a month after her death.


== Tributes ==
In 2019, Sosa was celebrated by a Google Doodle. The doodle was showcased in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Cuba, Iceland, Sweden, Serbia, Greece, Israel and Vietnam.
In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Sosa at number 160 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.

Musical artist  
  
**Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón** (9 July 1935[1] – 4 October 2009) was an
Argentine singer who was popular throughout [Latin
America](/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") and many countries outside the
region. With her roots in [Argentine folk music](/wiki/Folk_music_of_Argentina
"Folk music of Argentina"), Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of [El
nuevo cancionero](/wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n "Nueva canción"). She gave voice to
songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice
of the voiceless ones", [2] and often called "the conscience of Latin
America".[3]

Sosa performed in venues such as the [Lincoln Center](/wiki/Lincoln_Center
"Lincoln Center") in New York City, the [Théâtre
Mogador](/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador "Théâtre Mogador") in Paris, the
[Sistine Chapel](/wiki/Sistine_Chapel "Sistine Chapel") in Vatican City, as
well as sold-out shows in New York's [Carnegie Hall](/wiki/Carnegie_Hall
"Carnegie Hall") and the Roman [Colosseum](/wiki/Colosseum "Colosseum") during
her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the
recipient of six [Latin Grammy](/wiki/Latin_Grammy "Latin Grammy") awards
(2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a [Latin Grammy Lifetime
Achievement Award](/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Latin Grammy
Lifetime Achievement Award") in 2004 and two posthumous [Latin Grammy Award
for Best Folk Album](/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album "Latin
Grammy Award for Best Folk Album") in 2009 and 2011. She won the [Premio
Gardel](/wiki/Premios_Gardel "Premios Gardel") in 2000, the main musical award
in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for [UNICEF](/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF").

## Life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mercedes_Sosa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section:
Life")]

Sosa was born on 9 July 1935, in [San Miguel de
Tucumán](/wiki/San_Miguel_de_Tucum%C3%A1n "San Miguel de Tucumán"), in the
[northwestern Argentine](/wiki/Argentine_Northwest "Argentine Northwest")
province of [Tucumán](/wiki/Tucum%C3%A1n_Province "Tucumán Province"), of
[mestizo](/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") ancestry. She was of French, Spanish and
[Diaguita](/wiki/Diaguita "Diaguita") descent.[4] Her nickname "la negra",
which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is
a reference to her indigenous heritage.[5] Her parents, a day laborer and a
washerwoman,[3] were [Peronists](/wiki/Peronism "Peronism"), although they
never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the
[Peronist Party](/wiki/Peronist_Party "Peronist Party") in
[Tucuman](/wiki/Tucum%C3%A1n_Province "Tucumán Province") under the name
Gladys Osorio.[6] In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition
organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two
months.[7] She recorded her first album, _[La Voz de la
Zafra](/wiki/La_voz_de_la_zafra "La voz de la zafra")_ , in 1959.[7] A
performance at the 1965 [Cosquín National Folklore
Festival](/wiki/Cosqu%C3%ADn_Festival "Cosquín Festival")—where she was
introduced and brought to the stage while sitting in the audience by fellow
folk singer [Jorge Cafrune](/wiki/Jorge_Cafrune "Jorge Cafrune")—[8] brought
her to the attention of the Argentine public.[7] Sosa and her first husband,
[Manuel Oscar
Matus](/w/index.php?title=Manuel_Oscar_Matus&action=edit&redlink=1 "Manuel
Oscar Matus \(page does not exist\)"), with whom she had one son, were key
players in the mid-60s _[nueva canción](/wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n "Nueva
canción")_ movement (which was called _nuevo cancionero_ in Argentina).[9] Her
second record was _Canciones con Fundamento_ , a collection of Argentine folk
songs.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Mercedes_Sosa%2C_F%C3%A9lix_Luna_y_Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez.jpg/250px-
Mercedes_Sosa%2C_F%C3%A9lix_Luna_y_Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa,_F%C3%A9lix_Luna_y_Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez.jpg)Sosa
with [Félix Luna](/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Luna "Félix Luna") and [Ariel
Ramírez](/wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez "Ariel Ramírez") (at the piano)

Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the
cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much
bigger star" than her contemporaries.[10] In 1967, Sosa toured the United
States and Europe with great success.[_[citation
needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In
later years, she performed and recorded extensively, broadening her repertoire
to include material from throughout Latin America.

In the early 1970s, Sosa released two concept albums in collaboration with
composer [Ariel Ramírez](/wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez "Ariel Ramírez") and
lyricist [Félix Luna](/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Luna "Félix Luna"): _Cantata
Sudamericana_ and _Mujeres Argentinas_ (Argentine Women). She also recorded a
tribute to Chilean musician [Violeta Parra](/wiki/Violeta_Parra "Violeta
Parra") in 1971, including what was to become one of Sosa's signature songs,
_[Gracias a la vida](/wiki/Gracias_a_la_vida "Gracias a la vida")_.[4][11] She
further popularized of songs written by [Milton
Nascimento](/wiki/Milton_Nascimento "Milton Nascimento") of Brazil and [Pablo
Milanés](/wiki/Pablo_Milan%C3%A9s "Pablo Milanés") and [Silvio
Rodríguez](/wiki/Silvio_Rodr%C3%ADguez "Silvio Rodríguez") both from
[Cuba](/wiki/Cuba "Cuba").[4] Throughout the decade, she released albums such
as _Hasta la Victoria_ in 1972 and _Traigo un Pueblo_ _en mi Voz_ in 1973.
They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by [Ariel
Petrocelli](/w/index.php?title=Ariel_Petrocelli&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ariel
Petrocelli \(page does not exist\)") and Daniel Toro, which tackles political
and social issues like wealth and land inequality.[12][13] During the 1970s
she was a part of two films by the director [Leopoldo Torre
Nilsson](/wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson"): _[El Santo de
la Espada](/wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada "El Santo de la Espada")_ in 1970 and
_[Güemes, la tierra en armas](/wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas "Güemes:
la tierra en armas")_ in 1971, in which she portrayed [Juana Azurduy de
Padilla](/wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla "Juana Azurduy de Padilla"), the
guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence.[12][14]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg/250px-
Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg)Sosa in 1972

After the [military junta](/wiki/National_Reorganization_Process "National
Reorganization Process") of [Jorge Videla](/wiki/Jorge_Videla "Jorge Videla")
came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly
oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but
refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in [La
Plata](/wiki/La_Plata "La Plata") in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on
stage, along with all those attending the concert.[9] Their release came about
through international intervention.[7] Despite attempts to hold more concerts,
she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.[5] Banned in
her own country, she moved to Paris and then to [Madrid](/wiki/Madrid
"Madrid").[7][9] She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional
struggles during this period of her life.[5] While in exile, she released the
album _A Quien Doy_ in 1981. The album included a recording of the song
"Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific
Chilean singer/songwriter, [Patricio Manns](/wiki/Patricio_Manns "Patricio
Manns"). The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the
sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.[15] She related to this
feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview
with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of
morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".[5]

Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982,[16][9]
several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the
[Falklands War](/wiki/Falklands_War "Falklands War"), and gave a series of
concerts at the _[Teatro Ópera](/wiki/Teatro_Opera "Teatro Opera")_ in Buenos
Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A
[double album](/wiki/Double_album "Double album") of recordings, _[Mercedes
Sosa en Argentina](/wiki/Mercedes_Sosa_en_Argentina "Mercedes Sosa en
Argentina"),_ from these performances became an instant best seller. She then
traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these
performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country.[16] In
subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad,
performing in such venues as the [Lincoln Center](/wiki/Lincoln_Center
"Lincoln Center") in New York City and the _[Théâtre
Mogador](/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador "Théâtre Mogador")_ in Paris. In poor
health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in
1998.[7] In 1994, she played in the [Sistine Chapel](/wiki/Sistine_Chapel
"Sistine Chapel") in Vatican City.[4] In 2002, she sold out both [Carnegie
Hall](/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") in New York and the
[Colosseum](/wiki/Colosseum "Colosseum") in Rome in the same year.[4]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Mercedes_Sosa.jpg/250px-
Mercedes_Sosa.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa.jpg)Sosa in 1973

A supporter of [Perón](/wiki/Juan_Per%C3%B3n "Juan Perón"), she favored
leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President [Raul
Alfonsin](/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Alfons%C3%ADn "Raúl Alfonsín") in the election of
1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the
dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring"[17] She
opposed President [Carlos Menem](/wiki/Carlos_Menem "Carlos Menem"), who was
in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of [Néstor
Kirchner](/wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Kirchner "Néstor Kirchner"), who became president
in 2003.[18] Sosa was a [UNESCO Goodwill
Ambassador](/wiki/UNESCO_Goodwill_Ambassador "UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador") for
Latin America and the Caribbean.[9][19]

Sosa disliked being identified as a protest singer.[3][20] While she was
outright in her political stances, Sosa said the following on the position of
the artist:

> “An artist isn’t political in the party political sense – they have a
> constituency, which is their public – it is the poetry that matters most of
> all.”

In a career spanning four decades, she worked with performers across several
genres and generations, folk, opera, pop, rock, including [Martha

Baez"), [Francis Cabrel](/wiki/Francis_Cabrel "Francis Cabrel"), [Gal
Costa](/wiki/Gal_Costa "Gal Costa"), [Luz Casal](/wiki/Luz_Casal "Luz Casal"),
[Lila Downs](/wiki/Lila_Downs "Lila Downs"), [Lucio Dalla](/wiki/Lucio_Dalla
"Lucio Dalla"), [Maria Farantouri](/wiki/Maria_Farantouri "Maria Farantouri"),
[Lucecita Benitez](/wiki/Lucecita_Benitez "Lucecita Benitez"), [Nilda

Garcia](/wiki/Charly_Garcia "Charly Garcia"), [León

Sosa participated in a 1999 production of [Ariel
Ramírez](/wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez "Ariel Ramírez")'s _Misa Criolla_.[21] Her
song _Balderrama_ is featured in the 2008 movie _[Che](/wiki/Che_\(2008_film\)
"Che \(2008 film\)")_ , starring [Benicio del Toro](/wiki/Benicio_del_Toro
"Benicio del Toro") as the Argentine [Marxist](/wiki/Marxist "Marxist")
revolutionary [Che Guevara](/wiki/Che_Guevara "Che Guevara").[22]

Sosa was the co-chair of the [Earth Charter](/wiki/Earth_Charter "Earth
Charter") International Commission.

## Awards

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mercedes_Sosa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section:
Awards")]

Sosa won the [Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk
Album](/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album "Latin Grammy Award for
Best Folk Album") in 2000 (_Misa Criolla_),[23] 2003 (_Acústico_),[24] 2006
(_Corazón Libre_),[25] 2009 (_[Cantora 1](/wiki/Cantora,_un_Viaje_%C3%8Dntimo
"Cantora, un Viaje Íntimo")_ , which also won [Best Recording
Package](/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Recording_Package "Latin Grammy
Award for Best Recording Package") and was nominated for [Album of the
Year](/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Latin Grammy Award for
Album of the Year")),[26] and 2011 (_Deja La Vida Volar_),[27] as well as
several international awards.

In 1995, [Konex Foundation](/wiki/Konex_Foundation "Konex Foundation") from
Argentina granted her the Diamond [Konex Award](/wiki/Konex_Award "Konex
Award"), one of the most prestigious awards in Argentina, as the most
important personality in the popular music of her country in the last
decade.[28]

## Death

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mercedes_Sosa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section:
Death")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Funeral_de_Mercedes_Sosa.jpg/250px-
Funeral_de_Mercedes_Sosa.jpg)](/wiki/File:Funeral_de_Mercedes_Sosa.jpg)Mercedes
Sosa lying in repose, with her family and President [Cristina Fernández de
Kirchner](/wiki/Cristina_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_Kirchner "Cristina Fernández de
Kirchner") viewing

Suffering from recurrent [endocrine](/wiki/Endocrine_system "Endocrine
system") and [respiratory](/wiki/Respiratory_system "Respiratory system")
problems in later years, the 74-year-old Sosa was hospitalized in Buenos Aires
on 18 September 2009.[29] She died from [multiple organ
failure](/wiki/Multiple_organ_failure "Multiple organ failure") on 4 October
2009, at 5:15 am.[11] She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March
2019), born of her first marriage.[7][30] He said: "She lived her 74 years to
the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have
any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her".[30] The hospital
expressed its sympathies to her relatives.[31] Her website featured the
following: "Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions
leave a great legacy to future generations".[32]

Her body was placed on display at the [National
Congress](/wiki/Argentine_National_Congress "Argentine National Congress")
building in Buenos Aires for the public to pay their respects, and President
Fernández de Kirchner ordered three days of national mourning.[30][33]
Thousands had queued by the end of the day.[32][34]

Sosa's obituary in _[The Daily Telegraph](/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily
Telegraph")_ said she was "an unrivalled interpreter of works by her
compatriot, the Argentine [Atahualpa Yupanqui](/wiki/Atahualpa_Yupanqui
"Atahualpa Yupanqui"), and Chile's [Violeta Parra](/wiki/Violeta_Parra
"Violeta Parra")".[7] Helen Popper of [Reuters](/wiki/Reuters "Reuters")
reported her death by saying she "fought South America's dictators with her
voice and became a giant of contemporary Latin American music".[34] Sosa
received three [Latin Grammy](/wiki/Latin_Grammy "Latin Grammy") nominations
for her album, in 2009 . She went on to win Best Folk Album about a month
after her death.[4][9]

## Tributes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Mercedes_Sosa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section:
Tributes")]

In 2019, Sosa was celebrated by a [Google Doodle](/wiki/Google_Doodle "Google
Doodle"). The doodle was showcased in [Argentina](/wiki/Argentina
"Argentina"), [Chile](/wiki/Chile "Chile"), [Uruguay](/wiki/Uruguay
"Uruguay"), [Paraguay](/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"), [Bolivia](/wiki/Bolivia
"Bolivia"), [Peru](/wiki/Peru "Peru"), [Ecuador](/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador"),
[Cuba](/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), [Iceland](/wiki/Iceland "Iceland"), Sweden,
[Serbia](/wiki/Serbia "Serbia"), [Greece](/wiki/Greece "Greece"),
[Israel](/wiki/Israel "Israel") and [Vietnam](/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam").[35]

In 2023, _[Rolling Stone](/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked Sosa at
number 160 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.[36]

{'url': 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Sosa', 'title': 'Mercedes Sosa', 'content': 'Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón (9 July 1935 – 4 October 2009) was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout Latin America and many countries outside the region. With her roots in Argentine folk music, Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of El nuevo cancionero. She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice of the voiceless ones",  and often called "the conscience of Latin America".
Sosa performed in venues such as the Lincoln Center in New York City, the Théâtre Mogador in Paris, the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's Carnegie Hall and the Roman Colosseum during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six Latin Grammy awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2004 and two posthumous Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album in 2009 and 2011. She won the Premio Gardel in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for UNICEF.


== Life ==
Sosa was born on 9 July 1935, in San Miguel de Tucumán, in the northwestern Argentine province of Tucumán, of mestizo ancestry. She was of French, Spanish and Diaguita descent. Her nickname "la negra", which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is a reference to her indigenous heritage. Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman, were Peronists, although they never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the Peronist Party in Tucuman under the name Gladys Osorio. In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two months. She recorded her first album, La Voz de la Zafra, in 1959. A performance at the 1965 Cosquín National Folklore Festival—where she was introduced and brought to the stage while sitting in the audience by fellow folk singer Jorge Cafrune— brought her to the attention of the Argentine public. Sosa and her first husband, Manuel Oscar Matus, with whom she had one son, were key players in the mid-60s nueva canción movement (which was called nuevo cancionero in Argentina). Her second record was Canciones con Fundamento, a collection of Argentine folk songs.

Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries. In 1967, Sosa toured the United States and Europe with great success. In later years, she performed and recorded extensively, broadening her repertoire to include material from throughout Latin America.
In the early 1970s, Sosa released two concept albums in collaboration with composer Ariel Ramírez and lyricist Félix Luna: Cantata Sudamericana and Mujeres Argentinas (Argentine Women). She also recorded a tribute to Chilean musician Violeta Parra in 1971, including what was to become one of Sosa's signature songs, Gracias a la vida. She further popularized of songs written by Milton Nascimento of Brazil and Pablo Milanés and Silvio Rodríguez both from Cuba. Throughout the decade, she released albums such as Hasta la Victoria in 1972 and Traigo un Pueblo en mi Voz in 1973. They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by Ariel Petrocelli and Daniel Toro, which tackles political and social issues like wealth and land inequality. During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director Leopoldo Torre Nilsson: El Santo de la Espada in 1970 and Güemes, la tierra en armas in 1971, in which she portrayed Juana Azurduy de Padilla, the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence.

After the military junta of Jorge Videla came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in La Plata in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert. Their release came about through international intervention. Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime. Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to Madrid. She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life. While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter, Patricio Manns. The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland. She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982, several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the Falklands War, and gave a series of concerts at the Teatro Ópera in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A double album of recordings, Mercedes Sosa en Argentina, from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country. In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the Lincoln Center in New York City and the Théâtre Mogador in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998. In 1994, she played in the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City. In 2002, she sold out both Carnegie Hall in New York and the Colosseum in Rome in the same year.

A supporter of Perón, she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President Raul Alfonsin in the election of 1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring" She opposed President Carlos Menem, who was in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of Néstor Kirchner, who became president in 2003.
Sosa was a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Latin America and the Caribbean.
Sosa disliked being identified as a protest singer. While she was outright in her political stances, Sosa said the following on the position of the artist:

“An artist isn’t political in the party political sense – they have a constituency, which is their public – it is the poetry that matters most of all.”
In a career spanning four decades, she worked with performers across several genres and generations, folk, opera, pop, rock, including Martha Argerich, Andrea Bocelli, David Broza, Franco Battiato, Jaime Roos, Joan Baez, Francis Cabrel, Gal Costa, Luz Casal, Lila Downs, Lucio Dalla, Maria Farantouri, Lucecita Benitez, Nilda Fernández, Charly Garcia, León Gieco, Gian Marco, Nana Mouskouri, Pablo Milanés, Holly Near, Milton Nascimento, Pata Negra, Fito Páez, Franco De Vita, Lourdes Pérez, Luciano Pavarotti, Silvio Rodríguez, Ismael Serrano, Shakira, Sting, Caetano Veloso, Julieta Venegas, Gustavo Cerati and Konstantin Wecker
Sosa participated in a 1999 production of Ariel Ramírez's Misa Criolla. Her song Balderrama is featured in the 2008 movie Che, starring Benicio del Toro as the Argentine Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara.
Sosa was the co-chair of the Earth Charter International Commission.


== Awards ==
Sosa won the Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album in 2000 (Misa Criolla), 2003 (Acústico), 2006 (Corazón Libre), 2009 (Cantora 1, which also won Best Recording Package and was nominated for Album of the Year), and 2011 (Deja La Vida Volar), as well as several international awards.
In 1995, Konex Foundation from Argentina granted her the Diamond Konex Award, one of the most prestigious awards in Argentina, as the most important personality in the popular music of her country in the last decade.


== Death ==

Suffering from recurrent endocrine and respiratory problems in later years, the 74-year-old Sosa was hospitalized in Buenos Aires on 18 September 2009. She died from multiple organ failure on 4 October 2009, at 5:15 am. She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March 2019), born of her first marriage. He said: "She lived her 74 years to the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her". The hospital expressed its sympathies to her relatives. Her website featured the following: "Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions leave a great legacy to future generations".
Her body was placed on display at the National Congress building in Buenos Aires for the public to pay their respects, and President Fernández de Kirchner ordered three days of national mourning. Thousands had queued by the end of the day.
Sosa's obituary in The Daily Telegraph said she was "an unrivalled interpreter of works by her compatriot, the Argentine Atahualpa Yupanqui, and Chile's Violeta Parra". Helen Popper of Reuters reported her death by saying she "fought South America's dictators with her voice and became a giant of contemporary Latin American music". Sosa received three Latin Grammy nominations for her album, in 2009 . She went on to win Best Folk Album about a month after her death.


== Tributes ==
In 2019, Sosa was celebrated by a Google Doodle. The doodle was showcased in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Cuba, Iceland, Sweden, Serbia, Greece, Israel and Vietnam.
In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Sosa at number 160 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.

At the [North](/wiki/North_Pole "North Pole") and [South

[Zooplankton](/wiki/Zooplankton "Zooplankton") in the [Arctic](/wiki/Arctic
"Arctic") use [moonlight](/wiki/Moonlight "Moonlight") when the Sun is [below
the horizon](/wiki/Polar_night "Polar night") for months on end.[213]

The apparent orientation of the Moon depends on its position in the sky and
the hemisphere of the Earth from which it is being viewed. In the [Northern
Hemisphere](/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere "Northern Hemisphere") it appears upside
down compared to the view from the [Southern
Hemisphere](/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere "Southern Hemisphere").[214] Sometimes
the "horns" of a crescent moon appear to be pointing more upwards than
sideways. This phenomenon is called a [wet moon](/wiki/Wet_moon "Wet moon")
and occurs more frequently in the [tropics](/wiki/Tropics "Tropics").[215]

The [distance between the Moon and Earth](/wiki/Lunar_distance "Lunar
distance") varies from around 356,400 km (221,500 mi) ([perigee](/wiki/Perigee
"Perigee")) to 406,700 km (252,700 mi) (apogee), making the Moon's distance
and apparent size fluctuate up to 14%.[216][217] On average the Moon's
[angular diameter](/wiki/Angular_diameter "Angular diameter") is about 0.52°,
roughly the same apparent size as the Sun (see § Eclipses). In addition, a
purely psychological effect, known as the [Moon illusion](/wiki/Moon_illusion
"Moon illusion"), makes the Moon appear larger when close to the horizon.[218]

### Rotation

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Tidal_locking_of_the_Moon_with_the_Earth.gif/250px-
Tidal_locking_of_the_Moon_with_the_Earth.gif)](/wiki/File:Tidal_locking_of_the_Moon_with_the_Earth.gif)Comparison
between the Moon on the left, rotating tidally locked (correct), and with the
Moon on the right, without rotation (incorrect)

The [tidally locked synchronous rotation](/wiki/Synchronous_rotation
"Synchronous rotation") of the Moon as it orbits the Earth results in it
always keeping nearly the same face turned towards the planet. The side of the
Moon that faces Earth is called the [near side](/wiki/Near_side "Near side"),
and the opposite the [far side](/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the
Moon"). The far side is often inaccurately called the "dark side", but it is
in fact illuminated as often as the near side: once every 29.5 Earth days.
During [dark moon](/wiki/Dark_moon "Dark moon") to [new moon](/wiki/New_moon
"New moon"), the near side is dark.[219]

The Moon originally rotated at a faster rate, but early in its history its
rotation slowed and became [tidally locked](/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally
locked") in this orientation as a result of [frictional](/wiki/Friction
"Friction") effects associated with [tidal](/wiki/Tidal_force "Tidal force")
deformations caused by Earth.[220] With time, the energy of rotation of the
Moon on its axis was dissipated as heat, until there was no rotation of the
Moon relative to Earth. In 2016, planetary scientists using data collected on
the 1998–99 NASA _[Lunar Prospector](/wiki/Lunar_Prospector "Lunar
Prospector")_ mission found two hydrogen-rich areas (most likely former water
ice) on opposite sides of the Moon. It is speculated that these patches were
the poles of the Moon billions of years ago before it was tidally locked to
Earth.[221]

### Illumination and phases

See also: [Lunar phase](/wiki/Lunar_phase "Lunar phase"),
[Moonlight](/wiki/Moonlight "Moonlight"), and [Halo (optical
phenomenon)](/wiki/Halo_\(optical_phenomenon\) "Halo \(optical phenomenon\)")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Moon_phases_en.jpg/960px-
Moon_phases_en.jpg)](/wiki/File:Moon_phases_en.jpg)The monthly changes in the
angle between the direction of sunlight and view from Earth, and the [phases
of the Moon](/wiki/Lunar_phase "Lunar phase") that result, as viewed from the
[Northern Hemisphere](/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere "Northern Hemisphere"). The
[Earth–Moon distance](/wiki/Earth%E2%80%93Moon_distance "Earth–Moon distance")
is not to scale.

The Moon rotates, as it orbits Earth, changing orientation toward the Sun,
experiencing a [lunar day](/wiki/Lunar_day "Lunar day"). A lunar day is equal
to one [lunar month](/wiki/Lunar_month "Lunar month") (one synodic orbit
around Earth) due to it being [tidally locked](/wiki/Tidal_locking "Tidal
locking") to Earth. Since the Moon is not tidally locked to the Sun, lunar
daylight and night times both occur around the Moon. The changing position of
the illumination of the Moon by the Sun during a lunar day is observable from
Earth as the changing [lunar phases](/wiki/Lunar_phase "Lunar phase"), waxing
crescent being the sunrise and the waning crescent the sunset phase of a day
observed from afar.[222]

Lunar night is the darkest on the far side and during lunar eclipses on the
near side (and darker than a moonless night on Earth). During its night, the
near side is illuminated by [Earthlight](/wiki/Earthlight "Earthlight") to the
extent that lunar surface features may be observable from Earth. Earthshine
makes the night on the near side about 43 times brighter, and sometimes even
55 times brighter than a night on Earth illuminated by the light of the full
moon.[223]

In Earth's sky brightness and apparent size of the Moon changes also due to
its elliptic [orbit around Earth](/wiki/Orbit_of_the_Moon "Orbit of the
Moon"). At [perigee](/wiki/Perigee "Perigee") (closest), since the Moon is up
to 14% closer to Earth than at [apogee](/wiki/Apogee "Apogee") (most distant),
it subtends a [solid angle](/wiki/Solid_angle "Solid angle") which is up to
30% larger. Consequently, given the same phase, the Moon's brightness also
varies by up to 30% between apogee and perigee.[224] A full (or new) moon at
such a position is called a [supermoon](/wiki/Supermoon
"Supermoon").[216][217][225]

Each of the four intermediate phases of the Moon lasts, on average, about
seven days (approximately 7.38 days), but this duration can vary by about ±11%
due to the change in the distance between the Moon and Earth between apogee
(farthest point) and perigee (closest point).

The number of days since the most recent new moon is called the Moon's
age.[226] A complete cycle of lunar phases is known as a lunation.[227]

The approximate age and phase of the Moon for any date can be calculated by
determining the number of days since a known new moon (e.g., January 1, 1900,
or August 11, 1999) and dividing that value by the average length of a synodic
month (29.53059 days).[228] The remainder of the division represents the
Moon's age. This method assumes a perfectly circular orbit and does not
consider the exact time of the new moon, so results may be off by a few hours.
Accuracy decreases as the date moves away from the reference date.

This simplified calculation is suitable for general or decorative purposes,
such as moon phase clocks. More precise applications that take into account
the Moon's apogee and perigee require more complex methods.

Due to lunar libration, it is sometimes possible to see slightly more than the
full moon (up to about 101%) or a small part of its far side (up to 5%).[229]

#### Observational phenomena

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Lunar_impact_flash.jpg/250px-
Lunar_impact_flash.jpg)](/wiki/File:Lunar_impact_flash.jpg)[Lunar impact
flash](/wiki/Transient_lunar_phenomenon#Impact_flash "Transient lunar
phenomenon") image shown superimposed on the Moon

There has been historical controversy over whether observed features on the
Moon's surface change over time. Today, many of these claims are thought to be
illusory, resulting from observation under different lighting conditions, poor
[astronomical seeing](/wiki/Astronomical_seeing "Astronomical seeing"), or
inadequate drawings. However, [outgassing](/wiki/Outgassing "Outgassing") does
occasionally occur and could be responsible for a minor percentage of the
reported [lunar transient phenomena](/wiki/Lunar_transient_phenomena "Lunar
transient phenomena"). Recently, it has been suggested that a roughly 3 km
(1.9 mi) diameter region of the lunar surface was modified by a gas release
event about a million years ago.[230][231]

### Albedo and true color of the surface

The Moon's appearance is shaped by its reflective properties and surface
composition. Its [albedo](/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") is about 0.12,[232]
comparable to worn [asphalt](/wiki/Asphalt_concrete "Asphalt concrete"),
making it relatively dark despite its brightness in the night sky. This low
albedo represents the reflectance of the lunar regolith, a layer of fine rock
fragments created by meteorite impacts. Light scattering by the regolith
causes the Moon to appear much brighter at full moon than at quarter phases.

The Moon also exhibits retro-reflection,[233] scattering light back toward its
source and creating a uniform brightness across its disc without significant
limb darkening. Its apparent size and brightness vary due to its elliptical
orbit, appearing up to 30% brighter and 14% larger at perigee compared to
apogee, a phenomenon known as a "Supermoon".

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Two_Lunar_Phases.jpg/250px-
Two_Lunar_Phases.jpg)](/wiki/File:Two_Lunar_Phases.jpg)The changing apparent
color of the Moon, filtered by Earth's atmosphere

The Moon's true color, without atmospheric effects, is a muted brownish-
gray.[234] This results from silicate minerals in the regolith, with darker
basaltic plains (maria) and lighter feldspar-rich highlands. The maria, formed
by ancient volcanic flows, contain more iron and titanium, giving them a
darker tone.

From Earth, the Moon's color can be altered by the atmosphere, at times
appearing red or blue. It may appear red during a [lunar
eclipse](/wiki/Lunar_eclipse "Lunar eclipse"), because of the red spectrum of
the Sun's light being [refracted](/wiki/Refracted "Refracted") onto the Moon
by Earth's atmosphere. Because of this red color, lunar eclipses are also
sometimes called [blood moons](/wiki/Blood_Moon_\(eclipse\) "Blood Moon
\(eclipse\)"). The Moon can also seem red when it appears at low angles and
through a thick atmosphere.

The Moon may appear blue depending on the presence of certain particles in the
air,[235] such as volcanic particles,[236] in which case it can be called a
[blue moon](/wiki/Blue_moon#Whole_blue_moon "Blue moon").

Because the words "red moon" and "blue moon" can also be used to refer to
specific [full moons](/wiki/Full_moon "Full moon") of the year, they do not
always refer to the presence of red or blue [moonlight](/wiki/Moonlight
"Moonlight").

### Eclipses

Main articles: [Solar eclipse](/wiki/Solar_eclipse "Solar eclipse"), [Lunar
eclipse](/wiki/Lunar_eclipse "Lunar eclipse"), [Solar eclipses on the
Moon](/wiki/Solar_eclipses_on_the_Moon "Solar eclipses on the Moon"), and
[Eclipse cycle](/wiki/Eclipse_cycle "Eclipse cycle")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Solar_eclipse_1999_4.jpg/250px-
Solar_eclipse_1999_4.jpg)](/wiki/File:Solar_eclipse_1999_4.jpg)

A [solar eclipse](/wiki/Solar_eclipse "Solar eclipse") causes the Sun to be
covered, revealing the white [corona](/wiki/Stellar_corona "Stellar corona").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Full_Eclipse_of_the_Moon_as_seen_in_from_Irvine%2C_CA%2C_USA_%2852075715442%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-
Full_Eclipse_of_the_Moon_as_seen_in_from_Irvine%2C_CA%2C_USA_%2852075715442%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Full_Eclipse_of_the_Moon_as_seen_in_from_Irvine,_CA,_USA_\(52075715442\)_\(cropped\).jpg)

The Moon, tinted reddish, during a [lunar eclipse](/wiki/Lunar_eclipse "Lunar
eclipse")

Eclipses only occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are all in a straight line
(termed "[syzygy](/wiki/Syzygy_\(astronomy\) "Syzygy \(astronomy\)")"). [Solar
eclipses](/wiki/Solar_eclipse "Solar eclipse") occur at [new
moon](/wiki/New_moon "New moon"), when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.
In contrast, [lunar eclipses](/wiki/Lunar_eclipse "Lunar eclipse") occur at
full moon, when Earth is between the Sun and Moon. The apparent size of the
Moon is roughly the same as that of the Sun, with both being viewed at close
to one-half a degree wide. The Sun is much larger than the Moon, but it is the
vastly greater distance that gives it the same apparent size as the much
closer and much smaller Moon from the perspective of Earth. The variations in
apparent size, due to the non-circular orbits, are nearly the same as well,
though occurring in different cycles. This makes possible both
[total](/wiki/Total_eclipse "Total eclipse") (with the Moon appearing larger
than the Sun) and [annular](/wiki/Annular_eclipse "Annular eclipse") (with the
Moon appearing smaller than the Sun) solar eclipses.[237] In a total eclipse,
the Moon completely covers the disc of the Sun and the [solar
corona](/wiki/Solar_corona "Solar corona") becomes visible to the [naked
eye](/wiki/Naked_eye "Naked eye").

Because the distance between the Moon and Earth is very slowly increasing over
time,[198] the angular diameter of the Moon is decreasing. As it evolves
toward becoming a [red giant](/wiki/Red_giant "Red giant"), the size of the
Sun, and its apparent diameter in the sky, are slowly increasing.[l] The
combination of these two changes means that hundreds of millions of years ago,
the Moon would always completely cover the Sun on solar eclipses, and no
annular eclipses were possible. Likewise, hundreds of millions of years in the
future, the Moon will no longer cover the Sun completely, and total solar
eclipses will not occur.[238]

As the Moon's orbit around Earth is inclined by about 5.145° (5° 9′) to the
[orbit of Earth around the Sun](/wiki/Ecliptic "Ecliptic"), eclipses do not
occur at every full and new moon. For an eclipse to occur, the Moon must be
near the intersection of the two orbital planes.[239] The periodicity and
recurrence of eclipses of the Sun by the Moon, and of the Moon by Earth, is
described by the [saros](/wiki/Saros_\(astronomy\) "Saros \(astronomy\)"),
which has a period of approximately 18 years.[240]

Because the Moon continuously blocks the view of a half-degree-wide circular
area of the sky,[m][241] the related phenomenon of
[occultation](/wiki/Occultation "Occultation") occurs when a bright star or
planet passes behind the Moon and is occulted: hidden from view. In this way,
a solar eclipse is an occultation of the Sun. Because the Moon is
comparatively close to Earth, occultations of individual stars are not visible
everywhere on the planet, nor at the same time. Because of the
[precession](/wiki/Precession "Precession") of the lunar orbit, each year
different stars are occulted.[242]

### Moon illusion

This section is an excerpt from [Moon illusion](/wiki/Moon_illusion "Moon
illusion").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moon_illusion&action=edit)]

The [Moon illusion](/wiki/Moon_illusion "Moon illusion") is the [optical
illusion](/wiki/Optical_illusion "Optical illusion") of the Moon appearing
larger near the [horizon](/wiki/Horizon "Horizon") than it does higher up in
the [sky](/wiki/Sky "Sky"). It has been known since ancient times and recorded
by various cultures.[243][244]

### Pre-telescopic observation (before 1609)

It is believed by some that the oldest [cave paintings](/wiki/Cave_painting
"Cave painting") from up to 40,000 [BP](/wiki/Before_present "Before present")
of bulls and geometric shapes,[245] or 20–30,000 year old [tally
sticks](/wiki/Tally_stick "Tally stick") were used to observe the phases of
the Moon, keeping time using the waxing and waning of [the Moon's
phases](/wiki/Lunar_phases "Lunar phases").[246] Aspects of the Moon were
identified and aggregated in [lunar deities](/wiki/Lunar_deities "Lunar
deities") from [prehistoric times](/wiki/Prehistoric_times "Prehistoric
times") and were eventually documented and put into symbols from the very
first instances of [writing](/wiki/Writing "Writing") in the [4th millennium
BC](/wiki/4th_millennium_BC "4th millennium BC"). One of the earliest-
discovered possible depictions of the Moon is a 3,000 BCE rock carving
_Orthostat 47_ at [Knowth](/wiki/Knowth "Knowth"), Ireland.[247][248] The
crescent depicting the Moon as with the lunar deity
[Nanna/Sin](/wiki/Sin_\(mythology\) "Sin \(mythology\)") have been found from
the 3rd millennium BCE.[249]

The oldest named astronomer and poet [Enheduanna](/wiki/Enheduanna
"Enheduanna"), [Akkadian](/wiki/Akkadian_Empire "Akkadian Empire") high
priestess to the lunar deity Nanna/Sin and princess, daughter of [Sargon the
Great](/wiki/Sargon_the_Great "Sargon the Great") (c. 2334 - c. 2279 BCE), had
the Moon tracked in her chambers.[250] The oldest found and identified
depiction of the Moon in an astronomical relation to other astronomical
features is the [Nebra sky disc](/wiki/Nebra_sky_disc "Nebra sky disc") from
c. 1800–1600 BCE, depicting features like the [Pleiades](/wiki/Pleiades
"Pleiades") next to the Moon.[251][252]

disc](/wiki/Nebra_sky_disc "Nebra sky disc") (c. 1800–1600 BCE), found near a
possibly [astronomical complex](/wiki/Astronomical_complex "Astronomical
complex"), most likely depicting the Sun or full Moon, the Moon as a crescent,
the [Pleiades](/wiki/Pleiades "Pleiades") and the summer and winter solstices
as strips of gold on the side of the disc,[253][254] with the top representing
the [horizon](/wiki/Horizon "Horizon")[255] and [north](/wiki/North "North").

The [ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") philosopher
[Anaxagoras](/wiki/Anaxagoras "Anaxagoras") (d. 428 BC) reasoned that the Sun
and Moon were both giant spherical rocks, and that the latter reflected the
light of the former.[256][257]: 227 Elsewhere in the 5th century BC to 4th
century BC, [Babylonian astronomers](/wiki/Babylonian_astronomers "Babylonian
astronomers") had recorded the 18-year [Saros cycle](/wiki/Saros_cycle "Saros
cycle") of [lunar eclipses](/wiki/Lunar_eclipse "Lunar eclipse"),[258] and
[Indian astronomers](/wiki/Indian_astronomy "Indian astronomy") had described
the Moon's monthly elongation.[259] The [Chinese
astronomer](/wiki/Chinese_astronomer "Chinese astronomer") [Shi
Shen](/wiki/Shi_Shen "Shi Shen") ([fl.](/wiki/Fl. "Fl.") 4th century BC) gave
instructions for predicting solar and lunar eclipses.[257]: 411

In [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s (384–322 BC) [description of the
universe](/wiki/On_the_Heavens "On the Heavens"), the Moon marked the boundary
between the spheres of the mutable elements (earth, water, air and fire), and
the imperishable stars of [aether](/wiki/Aether_\(classical_element\) "Aether
\(classical element\)"), an [influential
philosophy](/wiki/Aristotelian_physics "Aristotelian physics") that would
dominate for centuries.[260] [Archimedes](/wiki/Archimedes "Archimedes")
(287–212 BC) designed a planetarium that could calculate the motions of the
Moon and other objects in the Solar System.[261] In the 2nd century BC,
[Seleucus of Seleucia](/wiki/Seleucus_of_Seleucia "Seleucus of Seleucia")
correctly thought that [tides](/wiki/Tide "Tide") were due to the attraction
of the Moon, and that their height depends on the Moon's position relative to
the [Sun](/wiki/Sun "Sun").[262] In the same century,
[Aristarchus](/wiki/On_the_Sizes_and_Distances_\(Aristarchus\) "On the Sizes
and Distances \(Aristarchus\)") computed the size and distance of the Moon
from Earth, obtaining a value of about twenty times the [radius of
Earth](/wiki/Radius_of_Earth "Radius of Earth") for the distance.

The Chinese of the [Han dynasty](/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") believed the
Moon to be energy equated to _[qi](/wiki/Qi "Qi")_ and their 'radiating
influence' theory recognized that the light of the Moon was merely a
reflection of the Sun; [Jing Fang](/wiki/Jing_Fang "Jing Fang") (78–37 BC)
noted the sphericity of the Moon.[257]: 413–414 [Ptolemy](/wiki/Ptolemy
"Ptolemy") (90–168 AD) greatly improved on the numbers of Aristarchus,
calculating a mean distance of 59 times Earth's radius and a diameter of 0.292
Earth diameters, close to the correct values of about 60 and 0.273
respectively.[263] In the 2nd century AD, [Lucian](/wiki/Lucian "Lucian")
wrote the novel _[A True Story](/wiki/A_True_Story "A True Story")_ , in which
the heroes travel to the Moon and meet its inhabitants. In 510 AD, the Indian
astronomer [Aryabhata](/wiki/Aryabhata "Aryabhata") mentioned in his
_[Aryabhatiya](/wiki/Aryabhatiya "Aryabhatiya")_ that reflected sunlight is
the cause of the shining of the Moon.[264][265] The astronomer and physicist
[Ibn al-Haytham](/wiki/Ibn_al-Haytham "Ibn al-Haytham") (965–1039) found that
[sunlight](/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight") was not reflected from the Moon like a
mirror, but that light was emitted from every part of the Moon's sunlit
surface in all directions.[266] [Shen Kuo](/wiki/Shen_Kuo "Shen Kuo")
(1031–1095) of the [Song dynasty](/wiki/Song_dynasty "Song dynasty") created
an allegory equating the waxing and waning of the Moon to a round ball of
reflective silver that, when doused with white powder and viewed from the
side, would appear to be a crescent.[257]: 415–416 During the [Middle
Ages](/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), before the invention of the telescope,
the Moon was increasingly recognized as a sphere, though many believed that it
was "perfectly smooth".[267]

### Telescopic exploration (1609–1959)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Galileo%27s_sketches_of_the_moon_%28cropped%29.png/250px-
Galileo%27s_sketches_of_the_moon_%28cropped%29.png)](/wiki/File:Galileo%27s_sketches_of_the_moon_\(cropped\).png)The
first published sketches of one of the first telescopic observations of the
Moon, from the paper _[Sidereus Nuncius](/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius "Sidereus
Nuncius")_ (1610) by [Galileo Galilei](/wiki/Galileo_Galilei "Galileo
Galilei"), providing among other findings the first descriptions of the Moon's
topography

The [telescope](/wiki/Telescope "Telescope") was developed and reported on in
1608. The first record of telescopic astronomy and rough mapping of the Moon's
features is from early summer 1609 by [Thomas Harriot](/wiki/Thomas_Harriot
"Thomas Harriot"), but which he did not publish. At the same time [Galileo
Galilei](/wiki/Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") too started to use
telescopes to observe the sky and the Moon, recording later that year more
detailed observations and crucial conclusions, such as that the Moon was not
smooth, featuring mountains and craters, which he published in 1610 in his
ground-breaking and soon widely discussed book _[Sidereus
Nuncius](/wiki/Sidereus_Nuncius "Sidereus Nuncius")_.

Later in the 17th century, the efforts of [Giovanni Battista
Riccioli](/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Riccioli "Giovanni Battista Riccioli") and
[Francesco Maria Grimaldi](/wiki/Francesco_Maria_Grimaldi "Francesco Maria
Grimaldi") led to the system of naming of lunar features in use today. The
more exact 1834–1836 _[Mappa Selenographica](/wiki/Mappa_Selenographica "Mappa
Selenographica")_ of [Wilhelm Beer](/wiki/Wilhelm_Beer "Wilhelm Beer") and
[Johann Heinrich von Mädler](/wiki/Johann_Heinrich_von_M%C3%A4dler "Johann
Heinrich von Mädler"), and their associated 1837 book _Der Mond_ , the first
[trigonometrically](/wiki/Trigonometry "Trigonometry") accurate study of lunar
features, included the heights of more than a thousand mountains, and
introduced the study of the Moon at accuracies possible in earthly
geography.[268] Lunar craters, first noted by Galileo, were thought to be
[volcanic](/wiki/Volcanic "Volcanic") until the 1870s proposal of [Richard
Proctor](/wiki/Richard_Proctor "Richard Proctor") that they were formed by
collisions.[76] This view gained support in 1892 from the experimentation of
geologist [Grove Karl Gilbert](/wiki/Grove_Karl_Gilbert "Grove Karl Gilbert"),
and from comparative studies from 1920 to the 1940s,[269] leading to the
development of [lunar stratigraphy](/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar
geologic timescale"), which by the 1950s was becoming a new and growing branch
of [astrogeology](/wiki/Astrogeology "Astrogeology").[76]

### First missions to the Moon (1959–1976)

See also: [Space Race](/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race") and [Moon
landing](/wiki/Moon_landing "Moon landing")

After [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") the first [launch
systems](/wiki/Launch_system "Launch system") were developed and by the end of
the 1950s they reached capabilities that allowed the [Soviet
Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and the [United
States](/wiki/United_States "United States") to launch
[spacecraft](/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft") into space. The [Cold
War](/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") fueled a closely followed development of
launch systems by the two states, resulting in the so-called [Space
Race](/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race") and its later phase the Moon Race,
accelerating efforts and interest in [exploration of the
Moon](/wiki/Exploration_of_the_Moon "Exploration of the Moon").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Luna_3_moon.jpg/250px-
Luna_3_moon.jpg)](/wiki/File:Luna_3_moon.jpg)First view of the [far side of
the Moon](/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), taken by [Luna
3](/wiki/Luna_3 "Luna 3"), October 7, 1959. Clearly visible is [Mare
Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense") (top right) and a mare
triplet of [Mare Crisium](/wiki/Mare_Crisium "Mare Crisium"), [Mare
Marginis](/wiki/Mare_Marginis "Mare Marginis") and [Mare
Smythii](/wiki/Mare_Smythii "Mare Smythii") (left center).

After the first spaceflight of [Sputnik 1](/wiki/Sputnik_1 "Sputnik 1") in
1957 during [International Geophysical
Year](/wiki/International_Geophysical_Year "International Geophysical Year")
the spacecraft of the Soviet Union's [_Luna_ program](/wiki/Luna_programme
"Luna programme") were the first to accomplish a number of goals. Following
three unnamed failed missions in 1958,[270] the first human-made object _[Luna
1](/wiki/Luna_1 "Luna 1")_ escaped Earth's gravity and passed the Moon on 4
January 1959. Later that year the first human-made object _[Luna
2](/wiki/Luna_2 "Luna 2")_ reached the Moon's surface by [intentionally
impacting](/wiki/Lander_\(spacecraft\)#Impactors "Lander \(spacecraft\)"). By
the end of the year _[Luna 3](/wiki/Luna_3 "Luna 3")_ reached as the first
human-made object the normally occluded [far side of the
Moon](/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), taking the first
photographs of it. The first spacecraft to perform a successful lunar [soft
landing](/wiki/Lander_\(spacecraft\) "Lander \(spacecraft\)") was _[Luna
9](/wiki/Luna_9 "Luna 9")_ and the first vehicle to orbit the Moon was _[Luna
10](/wiki/Luna_10 "Luna 10")_ , both in 1966.[76]

[![The small blue-white semicircle of Earth, almost glowing with color in the
blackness of space, rising over the limb of the desolate, cratered surface of
the Moon.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/NASA-
Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise.jpg/250px-NASA-
Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise.jpg)](/wiki/File:NASA-
Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise.jpg)_[Earthrise](/wiki/Earthrise "Earthrise")_ , by
NASA astronaut [William Anders](/wiki/William_Anders "William Anders"), the
first color [image of
Earth](/wiki/Timeline_of_first_images_of_Earth_from_space "Timeline of first
images of Earth from space") taken by a human from the Moon, during [Apollo
8](/wiki/Apollo_8 "Apollo 8") (1968), the first time a crewed spacecraft left
Earth orbit and reached another [astronomical body](/wiki/Astronomical_body
"Astronomical body")

Following President [John F. Kennedy](/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F.
Kennedy")'s 1961 commitment to a crewed Moon landing before the end of the
decade, the United States, under NASA leadership, launched a series of
uncrewed probes to develop an understanding of the lunar surface in
preparation for human missions: the [Jet Propulsion
Laboratory](/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory "Jet Propulsion Laboratory")'s
[Ranger program](/wiki/Ranger_program "Ranger program"), the [Lunar Orbiter
program](/wiki/Lunar_Orbiter_program "Lunar Orbiter program") and the
[Surveyor program](/wiki/Surveyor_program "Surveyor program"). The crewed
[Apollo program](/wiki/Apollo_program "Apollo program") was developed in
parallel; after a series of uncrewed and crewed tests of the Apollo spacecraft
in Earth orbit, and spurred on by a potential [Soviet lunar human
landing](/wiki/Soviet_human_lunar_programs "Soviet human lunar programs"), in
1968 [Apollo 8](/wiki/Apollo_8 "Apollo 8") made the first human mission to
lunar orbit (the first Earthlings, two tortoises, had circled the Moon three
months earlier on the Soviet Union's [Zond 5](/wiki/Zond_5 "Zond 5"), followed
by turtles on [Zond 6](/wiki/Zond_6 "Zond 6")).

The first time a person landed on the Moon and any extraterrestrial body was
when [Neil Armstrong](/wiki/Neil_Armstrong "Neil Armstrong"), the commander of
the American mission [Apollo 11](/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11"), set foot on the
Moon at 02:56 UTC on July 21, 1969.[271] Considered the culmination of the
[Space Race](/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race"),[272] an estimated 500 million
people worldwide watched the transmission by the [Apollo TV
camera](/wiki/Apollo_TV_camera "Apollo TV camera"), the largest television
audience for a live broadcast at that time.[273][274] While at the same time
another mission, the robotic sample return mission [Luna 15](/wiki/Luna_15
"Luna 15") by the Soviet Union had been in orbit around the Moon, becoming
together with Apollo 11 the first ever case of two extraterrestrial missions
being conducted at the same time.

The Apollo missions 11 to 17 (except [Apollo 13](/wiki/Apollo_13 "Apollo 13"),
which aborted its planned lunar landing) removed 380.05 kilograms (837.87 lb)
of lunar rock and soil in 2,196 [separate samples](/wiki/Moon_rock "Moon
rock").[275] Scientific instrument packages were installed on the lunar
surface during all the Apollo landings. Long-lived [instrument
stations](/wiki/Apollo_Lunar_Surface_Experiments_Package "Apollo Lunar Surface
Experiments Package"), including heat flow probes,
[seismometers](/wiki/Seismometer "Seismometer"), and
[magnetometers](/wiki/Magnetometer "Magnetometer"), were installed at the
[Apollo 12](/wiki/Apollo_12 "Apollo 12"), [14](/wiki/Apollo_14 "Apollo 14"),
[15](/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"), [16](/wiki/Apollo_16 "Apollo 16"), and
[17](/wiki/Apollo_17 "Apollo 17") landing sites. Direct transmission of data
to Earth concluded in late 1977 because of budgetary considerations,[276][277]
but as the stations' [lunar laser ranging](/wiki/Lunar_laser_ranging "Lunar
laser ranging") corner-cube retroreflector arrays are passive instruments,
they are still being used.[278] Apollo 17 in 1972 was the last crewed mission
to the Moon's orbit or surface, and the last to fly around the Moon until the
[Artemis II](/wiki/Artemis_II "Artemis II") lunar flyby in 2026. [Explorer
49](/wiki/Explorer_49 "Explorer 49") in 1973 was the last dedicated U.S. lunar
probe until 1994.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/AS12-48-7133_%2821470506269%29.jpg/250px-
AS12-48-7133_%2821470506269%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:AS12-48-7133_\(21470506269\).jpg)An
example of the robotic and human exploration of the Moon in the first [visit
of a separate mission](/wiki/Space_rendezvous "Space rendezvous") beyond [Low
Earth Orbit](/wiki/Low_Earth_Orbit "Low Earth Orbit") (1969),[279] [Apollo
12](/wiki/Apollo_12 "Apollo 12") astronaut [Pete Conrad](/wiki/Pete_Conrad
"Pete Conrad") checking on [Surveyor 3](/wiki/Surveyor_3 "Surveyor 3") at
their shared [lunar base](/wiki/Lunar_base "Lunar base"), with the Apollo 12
_Intrepid_ lander and S-band antenna in the distant background

The Soviet Union continued sending robotic missions to the Moon until 1976,
deploying in 1970 with [Luna 17](/wiki/Luna_17 "Luna 17") the first remote
controlled [rover](/wiki/Rover_\(space_exploration\) "Rover \(space
exploration\)") [Lunokhod 1](/wiki/Lunokhod_1 "Lunokhod 1") on an
extraterrestrial surface, and collecting and returning 0.3 kg of rock and soil
samples with three _Luna_ [sample return missions](/wiki/Sample_return_mission
"Sample return mission") (_[Luna 16](/wiki/Luna_16 "Luna 16")_ in 1970, _[Luna
20](/wiki/Luna_20 "Luna 20")_ in 1972, and _[Luna 24](/wiki/Luna_24 "Luna
24")_ in 1976).[280]

### Moon Treaty and explorational absence (1976–1990)

Main article: [Moon Treaty](/wiki/Moon_Treaty "Moon Treaty")

Following the [last Soviet mission to the Moon](/wiki/Luna_24 "Luna 24") of
1976, there was little further lunar exploration for fourteen years.
Astronautics had shifted its focus towards the exploration of the
[inner](/wiki/Inner_Solar_System "Inner Solar System") (e.g. [Venera
program](/wiki/Venera_program "Venera program")) and
[outer](/wiki/Outer_Solar_System "Outer Solar System") (e.g. [Pioneer
10](/wiki/Pioneer_10 "Pioneer 10"), 1972) [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System
"Solar System") [planets](/wiki/Planet "Planet"), but also towards [Earth
orbit](/wiki/Geocentric_orbit "Geocentric orbit"), developing and continuously
operating, beside [communication satellites](/wiki/Communication_satellite
"Communication satellite"), [Earth observation
satellites](/wiki/Earth_observation_satellite "Earth observation satellite")
(e.g. [Landsat program](/wiki/Landsat_program "Landsat program"), 1972),
[space telescopes](/wiki/Space_telescope "Space telescope") and particularly
[space stations](/wiki/Space_station "Space station") (e.g. [Salyut
program](/wiki/Salyut_program "Salyut program"), 1971).

Negotiation in 1979 of [Moon treaty](/wiki/Moon_treaty "Moon treaty"), and its
subsequent ratification in 1984 was the only major activity regarding the Moon
until 1990.

### Renewed exploration (1990–present)

In 1990 _[Hiten](/wiki/Hiten_\(spacecraft\) "Hiten \(spacecraft\)")_ –
_Hagoromo_ ,[281] the first dedicated lunar mission since 1976, reached the
Moon's orbit. Sent by Japan, it became the first lunar mission that was not a
Soviet Union or U.S. mission.

In 1994, the U.S. dedicated a mission to fly a spacecraft
(_[Clementine](/wiki/Clementine_\(spacecraft\) "Clementine \(spacecraft\)")_)
to the Moon again for the first time since 1973. This mission obtained the
first near-global topographic map of the Moon, and the first global
[multispectral](/wiki/Multispectral "Multispectral") images of the lunar
surface.[282] In 1998, this was followed by the _[Lunar
Prospector](/wiki/Lunar_Prospector "Lunar Prospector")_ mission, whose
instruments indicated the presence of excess hydrogen at the lunar poles,
which is likely to have been caused by the presence of water ice in the upper
few meters of the regolith within permanently shadowed craters.[283]

The next years saw a row of first missions to the Moon by a new group of
states actively exploring the Moon. Between 2004 and 2006 the first spacecraft
by the [European Space Agency](/wiki/European_Space_Agency "European Space
Agency") (ESA) ([SMART-1](/wiki/SMART-1 "SMART-1")) orbited the Moon,
recording the first detailed survey of chemical elements on the lunar
surface.[284] The [Chinese Lunar Exploration
Program](/wiki/Chinese_Lunar_Exploration_Program "Chinese Lunar Exploration
Program") reached the Moon for the first time with the orbiter _[Chang'e
1](/wiki/Chang%27e_1 "Chang'e 1")_ (2007–2009),[285] obtaining a full image
map of the Moon. [India](/wiki/Indian_Space_Research_Organisation "Indian
Space Research Organisation") reached, orbited, and impacted the Moon in 2008
for the first time with its [Chandrayaan-1](/wiki/Chandrayaan-1
"Chandrayaan-1") and [Moon Impact Probe](/wiki/Moon_Impact_Probe "Moon Impact
Probe"), becoming the fifth and sixth state to do so, creating a high-
resolution chemical, mineralogical and photo-geological map of the lunar
surface, and confirming the presence of [water molecules in lunar
soil](/wiki/Lunar_water "Lunar water").[286]

The U.S. launched the [Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
(LRO)](/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter "Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter") and
the [LCROSS](/wiki/LCROSS "LCROSS") impactor on June 18, 2009. LCROSS
completed its mission by making a planned and widely observed impact in the
crater [Cabeus](/wiki/Cabeus "Cabeus") on October 9, 2009,[287] whereas _LRO_
is currently in operation, obtaining precise lunar [altimetry](/wiki/Altimetry
"Altimetry") and high-resolution imagery.

China continued its lunar program in 2010 with [Chang'e 2](/wiki/Chang%27e_2
"Chang'e 2"), mapping the surface at a higher resolution over an eight-month
period, and in 2013 with [Chang'e 3](/wiki/Chang%27e_3 "Chang'e 3"), a lunar
[lander](/wiki/Lander_\(spacecraft\) "Lander \(spacecraft\)") along with a
[lunar rover](/wiki/Lunar_rover "Lunar rover") named
_[Yutu](/wiki/Yutu_\(rover\) "Yutu \(rover\)")_
([Chinese](/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 玉兔; lit. 'Jade
Rabbit'). This was the first lunar rover mission since _[Lunokhod
2](/wiki/Lunokhod_2 "Lunokhod 2")_ in 1973 and the first lunar [soft
landing](/wiki/Soft_landing "Soft landing") since _[Luna 24](/wiki/Luna_24
"Luna 24")_ in 1976, making China the third country to achieve this.

In 2014 the first privately funded probe, the [Manfred Memorial Moon
Mission](/wiki/Manfred_Memorial_Moon_Mission "Manfred Memorial Moon Mission"),
flew by the Moon. Another Chinese rover mission, [Chang'e 4](/wiki/Chang%27e_4
"Chang'e 4"), achieved the first landing on [the Moon's far
side](/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon") in early 2019.[288]
Also in 2019, India successfully sent its second probe,
[Chandrayaan-2](/wiki/Chandrayaan-2 "Chandrayaan-2"), to the Moon. In 2020,
China carried out its first robotic [sample return
mission](/wiki/Sample_return_mission "Sample return mission") ([Chang'e
5](/wiki/Chang%27e_5 "Chang'e 5")), bringing back 1,731 grams of lunar
material to Earth.[289]

The U.S. [developed plans](/wiki/Vision_for_Space_Exploration "Vision for
Space Exploration") for returning astronauts to the Moon beginning in
2004,[290] and with the signing of the U.S.-led [Artemis
Accords](/wiki/Artemis_Accords "Artemis Accords") in 2020, the [Artemis
program](/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") aims to return humans to the
Moon in the 2020s.[291] The Accords have been joined by a growing number of
countries. The introduction of the Artemis Accords has fueled a renewed
discussion about the international framework and cooperation of lunar
activity, building on the [Moon Treaty](/wiki/Moon_Treaty "Moon Treaty") and
the ESA-led [Moon Village](/wiki/Moon_Village "Moon Village")
concept.[292][293][294]

The equatorial radius of Earth is  6.378136 ⋅ 10 6 {\displaystyle 6.378136\cdot 10^{6}} ![{\\displaystyle 6.378136\\cdot 10^{6}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ae73b753c3cfce323498c075a7c14637b46fdaf4)[meters](/wiki/Metre "Metre"). Multiplying by  2 π {\displaystyle 2\pi } ![{\\displaystyle 2\\pi }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/73efd1f6493490b058097060a572606d2c550a06) to convert from equatorial radius to equatorial circumference results in  4.007501 ⋅ 10 7 {\displaystyle 4.007501\cdot 10^{7}} ![{\\displaystyle 4.007501\\cdot 10^{7}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b1d1cc448a2132e2a68af4f1898084790bb7285e) [meters](/wiki/Metre "Metre"), or  40075.01 k m {\displaystyle 40075.01km} ![{\\displaystyle 40075.01km}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5b61bba8ab93b974aebdfa9259d28750b3982388). Dividing the two results in a ratio of  9.59 {\displaystyle 9.59} ![{\\displaystyle 9.59}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/675ad51ed2a94499b068f673fa44682d250fe6e7). 
  10. **^** More accurately, the Moon's mean sidereal period (fixed star to fixed star) is 27.321661 days (27 d 07 h 43 min 11.5 s), and its mean tropical orbital period (from equinox to equinox) is 27.321582 days (27 d 07 h 43 min 04.7 s) (_Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Ephemeris_ , 1961, at p.107).
  11. **^** More accurately, the Moon's mean synodic period (between mean solar conjunctions) is 29.530589 days (29 d 12 h 44 min 02.9 s) (_Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Ephemeris_ , 1961, at p.107).
  12. **^** See graph in [Sun#Life phases](/wiki/Sun#Life_phases "Sun"). At present, the diameter of the Sun is increasing at a rate of about five percent per billion years. This is very similar to the rate at which the apparent angular diameter of the Moon is decreasing as it recedes from Earth.
  13. **^** On average, the Moon covers an area of 0.21078 square degrees on the night sky.
